cards.front: Three ways to estimate unpaid ULAE using the
cards.back:
Three ways to estimate unpaid ULAE using the generalized approach
1. Expected Claims approach: Unpaid ULAE = (W ∗ × L) − M
2. B-F approach: Unpaid ULAE = W ∗ × (L − B)
3. Development approach: Unpaid ULAE = M × (L/B − 1)

cards.front: Key assumptions of the Generalized Approach
cards.back:
• ULAE costs are proportional to the dollars of claims being
handled.
• ULAE amounts spent opening claims are proportional to
the ultimate cost of claims being reported.
• ULAE amounts spent maintaining claims are proportional
to payments made.
• ULAE amounts spent closing claims are proportional to the
ultimate cost of claims being closed.
Furthermore, the generalized approach also assumes that
there is no cost to re-open or re-close claims.

cards.front: One weakness of the generalized approach
cards.back:
It does not account for the case when ULAE inflation is
occurring at a different rate than claims inflation.

Additional assumptions of the Simplified Generalized Approach

cards.front: Key assumptions of the Classical Approach
cards.back:
• The ratio of paid ULAE to paid claims is stable and
approximates the true ULAE to claims ratio.
• For claims that have occurred, future ULAE costs will be
proportional to future claims payments.
• 50% of ULAE is paid when a claim is opened, and 50% of
ULAE is paid when a claim is closed.

cards.front: When the Classical Approach does not work well
cards.back:
The classical approach does not work well for long-tail
lines of business, in times when ULAE inflation rates differ
from claims inflation rates, when the insurer is significantly
growing or shrinking, or when the 50/50 assumption is not
appropriate.

cards.front: Claims basis formula under the Kittel Approach
cards.back:
B = (50% × CY Incurred Claims) + (50% × P)

(including IBNR)

cards.front: Unpaid ULAE formula for Classical and Kittel
cards.back:
Unpaid ULAE formula for Classical and Kittel approaches
Unpaid ULAE = W ∗ × [Pure IBNR + 50% × (Case + IBNER)]

cards.front: How the Kittel Approach is an improvement over the
cards.back:
How the Kittel Approach is an improvement over the Classical Approach
The Kittel approach is an improvement over the classical
approach when the book of business is growing or shrinking
and for longer tailed lines of business. This is because when
an insurer grows, ULAE tends to increase quickly, but the
claims from the additional exposures may not be paid for
many years (resulting in higher paid ULAE-to-paid claim
ratios). However, the reserves will start increasing sooner, so
including incurred claims will reduce this distortion.

cards.front: When the Kittel Approach does not work well
cards.back:
When the 50/50 assumption is not appropriate or when
ULAE inflation rates differ from claims inflation rates.

cards.front: How the Mango-Allen Approach differs from the
cards.back:
How the Mango-Allen Approach differs from the Classical Approach
The only difference between the Mango-Allen approach and
the classical approach is that expected paid claims are used
instead of actual paid claims when estimating the claims
basis for each year.
The Mango-Allen approach is useful when insurers have
limited or volatile calendar year paid claims. However, for
larger companies with more stable actual paid claims, the
extra effort to estimate the expected paid claims may not be
justified.

cards.front: Reasons for the development of the Generalized
cards.back:
Reasons for the development of the Generalized Approach
• Recognize an insurer’s rapid growth
• Be consistent with the insurer’s ULAE expenditures over
the life of a claim
• Reproduce key concepts underlying the Wendy Johnson
technique
• Use commonly available and reliable aggregate payment
and unpaid claims data
• Allow for alternatives to the 50/50 rule.

cards.front: Two issues in dollar-based techniques that are
cards.back:
Two issues in dollar-based techniques that are addressed by count-based
techniques
1. That ULAE is not directly proportional to claims (e.g., the
ULAE for a single $10,000 claim would be less than the
ULAE for ten $1,000 claims.)
2. That using ULAE-to-claims ratios results in volatile ULAE
when claims are volatile.

cards.front: Key assumption of and challenge with count-based
cards.back:
Key assumption of and challenge with count-based techniques
A key assumption of count-based techniques is that the same
kind of transaction costs the same ULAE regardless of claim
size.
A challenge with count-based techniques is obtaining
accurate and consistent claim count data.

cards.front: Briefly discuss the Brian technique
cards.back:
Brian assumed that ULAE would be split into 5 types of
transactions: opening claims, maintaining open claims,
making payments, closing claims, and reopening claims.
Brian then assumed that the ULAE costs for each of these
types of transactions was similar, and could be estimated
using historical ratios of ULAE to number of transactions.
One weakness of this technique is the assumption that all
transaction types require similar ULAE. A second more
important weakness is the difficulty in estimating the number
of future transactions as well as the average cost per
transaction.

cards.front: Briefly discuss the Johnson technique
cards.back:
Wendy Johnson assumed ULAE could be split into 2 types
of transactions: opening claims and maintaining claims.
Johnson then assumed that the ULAE costs for each of these
types of transactions could be estimated using historical
ratios of ULAE to number of transactions. However, unlike
Brian, Johnson allowed the costs per transactions to vary for
the different transaction types.
One benefit of Johnson’s approach was that only the relative
ULAE per transaction type was needed instead of the actual
ULAE.

cards.front: Briefly discuss the Mango-Allen Claim Staffing
cards.back:
Briefly discuss the Mango-Allen Claim Staffing Technique
Mango-Allen first calculated a new count base as Opened
claim counts + Closed claim counts + Pending (ending) open
claim counts (OCP). They calculated the workload for claims
adjusters as OCP counts per adjuster, and projected OCP
counts and divided by this workload (with any anticipated
adjustments) to get the projected number of claims adjusters.
Finally, they multiplied the projected number of adjusters by
the trended historical ULAE per claims adjuster to get the
ULAE reserve.
One concern with this approach is that the ULAE reserve
estimates are sensitive to the magnitude of the selected
parameters.

cards.front: Briefly discuss the Spalla approach
cards.back:
Spalla suggests that modern computer systems can now track
the time spent on individual claims by each claims employee.
This can be used to calculate the average ULAE per type
of transaction at different stages in a claim’s duration, and
these can be loaded for other ULAE costs (e.g., overhead).
Alternatively, instead of calculating the absolute cost per
transaction, a relative cost per transaction could also be
calculated.
